name: Hartle-Thorne Slowly Rotating Star
description: The gravitational field outside a slowly rotating star, through second order in its spin: Schwarzschild's exterior, the dragging of inertial frames, and a quadrupole moment set by the star's interior. Far from the star it is the field of Lense and Thirring, whose frame dragging Gravity Probe B measured around the Earth.
convention: The mass enters as the length $m = GM/c^2$ and the spin as the length $a = J/(Mc)$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Does a spinning body pull the space around it along? Albert Einstein thought so before general relativity was finished [pfister2007]. In June 1913 he and his friend Michele Besso computed, in the Entwurf theory that came before it, the Coriolis force inside a rotating shell of mass and the motion of the planets' nodes around a rotating Sun [pfister2007]. That September in Vienna he remarked that "unfortunately the expected effect is so small that we cannot hope to verify it in terrestrial experiments or in astronomy" [pfister2007].¶Hans Thirring first wanted to measure centrifugal forces inside a heavy rotating hollow cylinder, could not organize the equipment in the turmoil of the First World War, and turned to calculating the effect in general relativity [pfister2007]. His notebook of 1917, "Wirkung rotierender Massen", spends its first third mostly on centrifugal effects of second order in the angular velocity $\omega$ [pfister2007]. On 2 August 1917 Einstein wrote to him that a rotating shell also produces "a Coriolis field" that is "proportional to the first power of $\omega$", and added, "I have calculated this dragging for the earth; it stays far below any measurable amount" [pfister2007]. Thirring's next notebook pages, dated 5 and 11 September, take up that field [pfister2007].¶Thirring's paper on the rotating shell reached the publisher on 21 December 1917, and his paper with Josef Lense on the far field of a rotating sphere, and on the orbits of planets and moons in it, followed on 21 February 1918 [pfister2007, mashhoon1984]. In coordinates that are isotropic far from the body, their field is flat space with Newton's potential and one cross term, $ds^2 = -(1 - 2m/r)c^2dt^2 + (1 + 2m/r)(dr^2 + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2) - (4am/r)\sin^2\theta\,c\,dt\,d\phi$, where $m = GM/c^2$ is the mass and $a = J/(Mc)$ the angular momentum per unit mass [baines2021]. The 1918 papers have been in English since 1984, translated by Bahram Mashhoon, Friedrich Hehl, and Dietmar Theiss [mashhoon1984]. When Herbert Pfister went back to the notebook, the letters, and Einstein and Besso's manuscript in 2007, he concluded that "most of the merit for the so-called Lense-Thirring effect of general relativity belongs to Einstein" [pfister2007].¶Lense and Thirring worked only in the far field, a restriction that went in 1966, when Dieter Brill and Jeffrey Cohen treated slow rotation as a perturbation of Schwarzschild's geometry, with the mass "allowed to be comparable to its radius" [pfister2007, brill1966]. A year later James Hartle had the equations of structure for a whole rotating star, the rotation treated "to second order in the angular velocity, but no other approximation is made" [hartle1967]. His star drags observers around with it: $\omega$ in his metric is "the angular velocity acquired by an observer falling freely from infinity", and outside the star it is $2amc/r^3$ [hartle1967]. He and Kip Thorne then built white dwarfs, neutron stars, and supermassive stars from those equations, and their models reached the journal on 12 January 1968, six weeks before Antony Hewish, Jocelyn Bell, and their colleagues announced the first pulsar [hartlethorne1968, hewish1968].¶Outside the star Hartle and Thorne's line element holds only three constants, "the total mass of the rotating star", "the star's total angular momentum", and "the star's mass quadrupole moment", and it "describes correctly the geometry outside any slowly rotating configuration" [hartlethorne1968]. Kerr's black hole is the case $Q = J^2/M$, a relation that, they wrote, "shows the very special nature of the Kerr solution" [hartlethorne1968, kerr1963]. A neutron star's quadrupole moment is larger: in William Laarakkers and Eric Poisson's numerical models of 1999 it is between $2.0$ and $12.1$ times Kerr's at the same mass and spin, depending on the mass and the equation of state [laarakkers1999]. How far can second order be trusted? In 2005 Emanuele Berti, Frances White, Asimina Maniopoulou, and Marco Bruni matched Hartle and Thorne's stars to numerical solutions of the full Einstein equations and found the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit "accurate to better than 1%, even for the fastest observed ms pulsar", and the quadrupole moment good to about 20% at the same rotation rates [berti2005].¶A gyroscope in orbit has its axis turned by the Earth's rotation, by 42 milliarcseconds a year, and George Pugh in 1959 and Leonard Schiff in 1960 each proposed flying one [pfister2007, everitt2011, schiff1960]. Ignazio Ciufolini and Erricos Pavlis went by Lense and Thirring's own route, the orbits of satellites, and their 2004 result for two Earth satellites is "99 ± 5 per cent of the value predicted by general relativity" [ciufolini2004]. Gravity Probe B went up on 20 April 2004 into a polar orbit 642 km high, and from its four gyroscopes Francis Everitt's team got a frame dragging drift of $-37.2 \pm 7.2$ milliarcseconds per year, where general relativity predicts $-39.2$ [everitt2011]. The dragging turned up outside the solar system in 2020, when Vivek Venkatraman Krishnan and his colleagues attributed the slow change in the inclination of the orbit of the pulsar PSR J1141-6545 to its fast rotating white dwarf companion, part of it through the star's quadrupole moment and part through frame dragging [venkatraman2020].¶A new chart came in 2021 from Joshua Baines, Thomas Berry, Alex Simpson, and Matt Visser, who wrote the first order field as $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + (dr + \sqrt{2m/r}\,c\,dt)^2 + r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,(d\phi - (2am/r^3)\,c\,dt)^2)$, with unit lapse and "flat spatial slices" [baines2021]. An observer dropped from rest far away with no angular momentum, on what they call a "rain" geodesic, falls inward at $\sqrt{2m/r}\,c$ and is carried around at $2amc/r^3$, and the chart's $t$ is that observer's own clock [baines2021]. Their line element solves the vacuum equations only to first order in $a$: its Ricci scalar is $18a^2m^2\sin^2\theta/r^6$, and its Weyl tensor is of Petrov type I [baines2021]. They offer it "in its own right" as a "black hole mimic" for observational astronomers [baines2021].

related.text: The black hole is the star with $q = a^2$. Kerr's metric expanded to second order in $a$ is Hartle and Thorne's with that quadrupole moment, after a change of $r$ and $\theta$ [hartlethorne1968].
Hartle and Thorne's star with the spin switched off. At $a = 0$ and $q = 0$ the field is Schwarzschild's.
The star before it turns. Hartle built his rotating star as a perturbation of this one, and Hartle and Thorne's field is the outside of the result [hartle1967].
A rotating fluid in closed form that no such exterior fits. Expanded to second order in its rotation, Wahlquist's interior cannot be joined to an asymptotically flat vacuum [bradley2000].

A rotating body solved exactly, a disc of dust at any speed of rotation. Bardeen and Wagoner took it up because studies such as Hartle and Thorne's had assumed slow rotation or weak fields [bardeen1969].

Lense and Thirring's weak field with numbers in front of its terms, so that other theories of gravity fit in it too. The dragging of frames comes with the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \gamma + \tfrac{1}{4}\alpha_1)$, which is $1$ in general relativity [will2014].

An exact static field with a mass and a quadrupole moment. To first order in its quadrupole parameter it is Hartle and Thorne's exterior without rotation, after a stretch by Zipoy and Voorhees's $\delta$ and a change of coordinates [boshkayev2019].

coordinates.name: Hartle-Thorne
domains: r = R \;\text{(the surface of the star)}

parameters.description: Mass of the rotating star as a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Spin per unit mass, $a = J/(Mc)$ with $J$ the angular momentum, a length
Mass quadrupole moment per unit mass, $q = Q/M$, an area, positive for an oblate star; Kerr's value is $q = a^2$
Radius of the star's surface, with $R > 2m$; the star itself fills $r < R$
The logarithm in Hartle and Thorne's two Legendre functions of the second kind
Hartle and Thorne's $\tfrac{5}{8}Q_2^{\,2}(r/m - 1)$, which falls off as $m^3/r^3$
Schwarzschild's $1 - 2m/r$ with the second order term of the spin
Quadrupole part of $g_{tt}$; far from the star $h_2 \to qm/r^3$

coordinates.convention: We use Hartle and Thorne's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and count $a$ as first order and $q$ as second. The metric and its inverse are written whole, and the connection and curvature keep terms through second order. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

The inverse metric, the connection, and the curvature keep terms through first order. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Joshua Baines, Thomas Berry, Alex Simpson, and Matt Visser, whose $t$ carries dimensions of time and is the proper time of an observer falling from rest far away with no angular momentum. Every component is exact for the line element as written, which agrees with Hartle and Thorne's to first order in $a$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
